newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. monetary policy tightening an issue for APEC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. monetary policy tightening an issue for APEC.

text.p: United States monetary policy as well as the dollar/yen exchange rate were issues that should be discussed by finance ministers of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, the International Monetary Fund said.
Finance ministers of the 18 member economies of APEC are to gather in Cebu in the central Philippines for a two-day meeting beginning on Saturday.

An IMF paper to be presented at the meeting, a copy of which was seen by Reuters on Thursday, cautioned APEC ministers, saying the "continued balanced growth with low inflation in the United States is important for the health of the APEC region".

"How do ministers view the recent tightening of monetary policy in the United States, and prospects for and potential consequences of further tightening, should that appear warranted to contain inflationary risks?" the paper asked.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised its federal funds rate on March 25 to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent.
"Is there a risk of a major stock market correction in the United States that would have significant repercussions in other APEC countries?", the paper said.

The APEC ministers are due to discuss ways to free capital flows in the region, to suggest measures to develop the capital and financial markets and encourage private sector investments in infrastructure.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus is to attend the meeting.
The IMF also suggested discussions on the dollar/yen exchange rate, saying sharp fluctuations in the values of the two currencies against each other had affected some APEC countries adversely.
"The large change in the yen/dollar rate has accentuated the real effective exchange rate appreciation for several APEC economies that maintain relatively close links to the U.S. dollar.

"This appreciation has helped restrain demand pressures, but it has exacerbated current account deficits in some countries. Do ministers agree that current account deficits in some APEC emerging market economies are excessive?
"In addition to considering further exchange rate flexibility, do ministers see a role for additional fiscal consolidation in addressing demand pressures?" the IMF said.
The IMF said greater exchange rate flexibility vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar could be helpful.

The IMF cited the example of the Thai baht, saying its real effective exchange rate had appreciated strongly since 1995 at a time when the current account deficit remained large, at eight percent of gross domestic product.
The IMF said the yen's fall to the level before its surge in 1992 had corrected misalignments, and some of the depreciation of the Japanese currency may be reversed.

"Exchange rate movements have generally continued the trends evident since the summer of 1995. In real effective terms, the dollar is at the peak of its trading range observed since the start of the decade, while the yen has fallen back to its level before its upsurge in 1992.
"These exchange rate changes...are consistent with underlying fundamentals and relative cyclical positions.
"As cyclical positions become less divergent, some of the recent depreciation of the yen may be reversed," it said.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
